title: Leeman's progress report on his research
summary: Leeman says he has worked five days at ten to twelve hours daily on his notes, is a third of the way done, and apologizes for repeating superlatives.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: This is Wednesday, February 28th. My fifth day into the project. I'm now putting in 10 to 12 hours daily on this research, and I find myself researching me and not circumstances -- but I have to dig in all these papers I'm saddled with here, in order to pick up the most important facts of interest and discard the unimportant.

The listener will never know the hours this takes. This is my fourth day at home, and my fifth day, as I said, including the day with you, Milton, and I'm only into about a third of what I would eventually like to call a fairly complete synopsis of my life and music. There will be so much left unsaid because of the time limit we have to work in. I have yet to get to the episodes ahead that were, to me, the best and most satisfying accomplishments of my life. The fifties through the present, 1979. And the highlights and bands and stars I was associated with.
If I were an English major, I would make better

listening -- period. I'm running out of superlatives -- wonderful and the great, for instance. You've got to take in to context that the musicians that I worked with over the years were the greatest, that I'm referring to, and were the most wonderful in their fields, and as I say, if I were an English major, I would probably research in the dictionary to use other superlatives. However, you'll have to take my repetition, and we'll go from there. We don't have time to research a dictionary.

Right, Cliff, we don't have time to research a dictionary -- we just want your story the way you tell it, and we're not looking for an English major. You are the major, Cliff Leeman, the great drummer. And we'll take a break now and change tapes.
